newsitem.title: USA: Company recalls berries after U.S. hepatitis scare.
newsitem.headline: Company recalls berries after U.S. hepatitis scare.

text.p: Anderson & Williams, which distributed frozen strawberries that may have exposed 9,000 Los Angeles students to the hepatitis A virus began a voluntary recall of the possibly tainted fruit on Wednesday.
The berries were also thought to be responsible for a recent outbreak of hepatitis A in some schools in Michigan.
The fruit, packaged in cups and which the company said was grown in Mexico -- which would be illegal -- was also shipped to four other states; Illinois, Iowa, Florida and Arizona.

The fruit was distributed as part of a Department of Agriculture-sponsored school meals programme by the San Diego firm of Anderson & Williams, a processor and packer of foods. Companies are required by law to certify in writing that the products sold to the programme are grown in the United States.

Separately, Agriculture Department sources, who declined to name the distributor of the strawberries, said the agency is investigating whether the tainted fruit came from Mexico. They also said 17 states got the strawberries, including six states that got the same lot.
The firm's parent company, Epitope Inc., based in Beaverton, Ore., announced Wednesday that Anderson & Williams would recall 13 lots of strawberries that were shipped early in December.

"The health and well-being of the public is A&W's foremost concern," Epitope Chief Executive Adolph Ferro said. "While it is not certain that the lots being recalled are contaminated, we want to eliminate all possible risk to consumers."
He said customers had been notified and the company was cooperating with the Centres for Disease Control and the Food and Drug Administration.
Meanwhile, health officials in Los Angeles were preparing Wednesday to offer inoculations to the 9,000 students at 18 elementary, middle and high schools who may have been exposed to the virus.

"It's not a panic situation," stressed Dr. Shirley Fannin, the Los Angeles County director of infectious diseases. She added that hepatitis A has an incubation period of 14 days and the strawberries were consumed last week.
"We're here within a week of consumption. We have another week to plan," she said.

In Chicago, school officials said they did not believe that any of the cases of strawberries shipped to schools there had been consumed, but were still checking, adding that strawberries were not on any school menus recently.
They said that out of the 1,320 cases sent to Chicago from the California supplier, 971 were still in warehouse and there were no known cases of hepatitis among Chicago students.

Just how the hepatitis A virus got into the strawberries was being investigated Wednesday by federal officials from the National Centre for Infectious Diseases, a unit of the Centres for Disease Control in Atlanta.
Hepatitis A is easily spread through uncooked food and typically causes a mild liver infection. Symptoms include fatigue, vomiting, abdominal discomfort and jaundice.
The drug gamma globulin has proved to be effective in preventing the disease if administered within 14 days of consumption of tainted food.
Epitope's stock fell $1.125 to $9 on Nasdaq in early afternoon trading.
